Front of House 101

The front of house is, as you might have guessed, the front of the restaurant. It's where patrons dine or are greeted at the front door. Also included in the front of house are the hostess station, bar, restrooms, and outdoor seating, if you have it.

Rebuilding a healthier culture at a family casual restaurant starts with recognizing that the biggest predictor of turnover is not pay alone but how people are managed day to day. Industry survey data collected by Toast found that among restaurant employees who recently quit, 45 percent cited a bad manager as the top factor, ahead of low pay, lack of recognition, and schedule complaints. That same data shows lack of recognition for hard work is nearly as common a reason for leaving as pay itself, so before writing any values statement, the first concrete move is to change how you personally show up as a manager: consistent, predictable, and responsive rather than reactive. A useful first-week action is to sit with both FOH and BOH separately and simply ask where the friction actually happens, because conflict specialists who work exclusively with restaurants find the same handful of triggers everywhere: servers "stacking" tickets so the kitchen gets slammed all at once, cooks reacting defensively when food gets sent back, and each side believing it is under more pressure than the other. Naming these patterns out loud, in a shift meeting rather than a poster, is itself a culture intervention, because staff who feel unheard by management are the ones most likely to quietly disengage and leave. Once you know your specific trigger points, build them into onboarding and daily routine rather than leaving them to chance: teach new servers explicitly how to stagger orders instead of dumping them, and teach cooks how to communicate a remake without treating the server as the enemy. A low-cost, high-impact next step is a literal job swap for a shift, having a server run a cold station during a rush and a cook shadow the floor on a busy night, which is designed purely to build empathy without disrupting service, since you choose positions that will not turn the shift upside down. Pairing that with something as simple as a shared staff meal before service gives both sides low-stakes time together outside the pressure of a rush, which restaurant operators report meaningfully shifts the "us versus them" dynamic between kitchen and floor. Because your kitchen staff resents inconsistent, chaotic ticket flow and your servers resent inconsistent schedules, the underlying fix for both is the same discipline: make the shift experience predictable. Restaurant retention consultants argue that assigning comparable workloads and consistent expectations shift after shift reduces anxiety far more than any single perk, because staff who don't know whether they're walking into a slammed section or an easy one carry stress into every shift. That means last-minute schedule changes should become the exception you actively track and explain, not a normal operating pattern, since unpredictability is functionally the same burnout driver as an unfair workload split. On the money side, tip-sharing between FOH and BOH is one of the few structural levers that directly addresses the "servers versus kitchen" resentment, because it recognizes that both sides contribute to the guest experience and narrows the pay gap that fuels bad blood. It is not without friction of its own, since it requires FOH buy-in and administrative effort to run fairly, but operators who implement it report real gains in cross-team morale and even help recruiting for kitchen roles. Toast's research similarly points to splitting incentive programs across both departments, tying FOH rewards to sales or table turns and BOH rewards to waste reduction or other kitchen metrics, so recognition isn't perceived as one-sided. The comment from your younger staff that customer feedback gets "brushed off because that's just restaurant life" deserves direct attention, because normalized dismissiveness toward complaints is closely tied to the same normalization that lets harassment slide unaddressed. Research on restaurant workers found that once employees are trained to treat hostile customer behavior as routine, they generalize that tolerance into other jobs and their personal lives, meaning your current culture of "brushing off" comments may already be teaching staff to underreport real problems, including harassment. This is not an abstract risk in food service specifically: federal data shows workers in accommodation and food services accounted for 14 percent of all EEOC harassment charges, disproportionate to the sector's share of employment, and a Restaurant Opportunities Center survey found tipped servers paid the $2.13 subminimum wage were about twice as likely to report sexual harassment as servers earning full minimum wage plus tips. One operator's practical fix worth adapting at smaller scale is a color-coded escalation system, where staff flag early "testing the waters" behavior from customers and management has a defined, no-questions-asked response ready before it escalates, rather than leaving each server to decide in the moment whether a comment is worth raising. Separately, data suggests that paying workers closer to full minimum wage rather than relying entirely on tips is associated with roughly half the harassment rate, which is a meaningful data point even if a full wage-model change isn't feasible immediately. Given all of this, the sequence that avoids "blowing up the business" while still producing real change is: first, fix your own management consistency and workload predictability since that is the single largest lever on turnover; second, formalize FOH-BOH friction points into onboarding and build in job-swap and shared-meal touchpoints; third, stand up an explicit, low-drama protocol for customer complaints and harassment so staff know exactly what happens when they report something instead of absorbing it; and fourth, once trust is rebuilding, revisit tip-sharing or incentive structures as the financial signal that FOH and BOH are genuinely one team. None of this requires a poster on the wall, because the evidence consistently points to management behavior, workload predictability, and how complaints are actually handled as the real culture, not the stated one.
